parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀφορίζω (aphorízō), probably through a Slavic intermediary.
From Byzantine Greek αγίασμα (agíasma), possibly partly through the intermediate of South Slavic or Old Church Slavonic. Compare Aromanian agiazma, Albanian ajazmë.

Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”), partly through South Slavic, or Old Church Slavonic архиепискоупъ (arxijepiskupŭ); compare Serbo-Croatian and Bulgarian архиѐпископ. Equivalent to arhi- + episcop.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀρχοντολόγιον (arkhontológion).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀρχονταρεῖον (arkhontareîon).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis) or French catéchèse. Doublet of catihis.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κῦρ (kûr).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek δηνάριον (dēnárion), from Latin denarius. Doublet of denar.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek δραγομάνος (dragomános), from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān), from Classical Syriac ܬܰܪܓܡܳܢܳܐ (targmānā), from Akkadian 𒅴𒁄 (targumannum, “interpreter”).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek χρονικόν (khronikón).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἴσον (íson).

parole.significato: A common expression used on a variety of holidays and other occasions, corresponding, depending on the case, to happy N…
parole.testo: Literally, “to/for many years”. Calque of Byzantine Greek εἰς ἔτη πολλά (eis étē pollá). Compare Bulgarian за много години (za mnogo godini), Albanian për shumë vjet, Serbo-Croatian за много годинa, Aromanian ti multsã anj.

parole.significato: an administrative position in the medieval Romanian principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia, such as the chief ministe…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek or Byzantine Greek λογοθέτης (logothétēs) (see English logothete), partially through the intermediate of South Slavic logotetĭ, logofetĭ, cf. also Turkish loğofet.

From Byzantine Greek ὄργανος (órganos), from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon), partly through the intermediate of Old Church Slavonic оръганъ (orŭganŭ). Some senses also based on French orgue (cf. orgă), Latin organum, Italian organo.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek παλάτι (paláti), from Latin palātium. Doublet of polată.

parole.significato: unleavened bread for Passover; azyme; matzo
parole.testo: Probably from Byzantine Greek πάσχα (páskha). Less likely from Latin pascha or through a Slavic intermediate pascha. Compare also the related Paște (“Easter”).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek πάθημα (páthēma).
Derived from Byzantine Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face”). Compare Aromanian prusopi.

parole.significato: a kind of high nobility in the feudal Romanian principalities, also the chief of the army
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σπάθαριος (spátharios), itself derived from Late Latin spatharius, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ὀστράκινος (ostrákinos), derived from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon).
Unknown. Possibly a substratum word, or, alternatively from Byzantine Greek θόρυβος (thórubos, “noise”) (whence Albanian tërboz (“noise”), tërboj (“to rage”)).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek οὐρανίσκος (ouranískos).

Borrowed from Byzantine Greek or Greek βενετικός (venetikós, “Venetian”). Compare also Aromanian venetic, Turkish venedik, Albanian venetik, Slavic venedikŭ. In Romanian, the word can occasionally carry the connotation of being foreign in a religious sense. The meaning may go back ultimately to Crus
From Byzantine Greek βλαστάριον (vlastárion), through the intermediate of Bulgarian властара (vlastara), властари (vlastari).

parole.significato: a mythical powerful bird-like creature, often with two heads
parole.testo: From the form gripsor, from Byzantine Greek γρύψ (grúps), from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps) (whence ultimately also grifon, borrowed through French). The final -or may result from the plural of an original form *grips > *gripsuri.

Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ζιζάνια (zizánia), from Ancient Greek ζιζάνια (zizánia), ζιζάνιον (zizánion, “type of weed, probably darnel”). Compare French zizanie. See also semantic evolution of sălbăție.
